abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cancer patients prone to toxicities might benefit from dose reduction over fixed‐dose recommendations. We develop a predictive index to identify patients with increased probability of dose reduction, intolerable toxicities, or therapy discontinuation (hereafter: dose reduction) in metastatic breast cancer (MBC) and compare real‐world effectiveness of reduced (RSD) versus full starting dose (FSD) using this index. This analysis included 618 patients with HR‐positive, HER2‐negative MBC from the prospective, observational, multicenter registry OPAL (NCT03417115), receiving first‐line palbociclib (n = 386) or ribociclib (n = 232) plus endocrine therapy. A logistic regression model was employed to derive the predictive index. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to emulate a head‐to‐head comparison of RSD and FSD by analyzing progression‐free (PFS) and overall survival (OS). Within 6 months, 215 patients (35%) underwent dose reduction, including 109 (51%) with RSD. Predictors for dose reduction were age ≥65 years and Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) ≥1. Among patients with increased probability of dose reduction (index ≥1: ≥65 years and/or CCI ≥ 1), median PFS and OS were 30.1 [21.7, 54.0] and 57.6 [40.0, NA] months with RSD vs. 29.3 [24.9, 32.0] and 43.1 [38.8, 50.3] months with FSD. For low‐probability patients (index = 0: <65 years and CCI = 0), median PFS and OS were 17.6 [9.1, 29.8] and 32.9 [23.1, 40.9] months with RSD vs. 24.5 [19.8, 32.0] and 54.2 [48.8, NA] months with FSD. In this real‐world MBC setting, patients ≥65 years and/or with CCI ≥ 1 had an increased probability of dose reduction and may benefit from RSD, as this yielded outcomes comparable to FSD. Younger, fitter patients may require full dosing. Future studies, ideally randomized controlled trials, should aim to confirm these findings.

sec.p: Keywords: breast neoplasms, dose reduction, palbociclib, predictive index, registries, ribociclib

abstract.title: What's New?
abstract.p: Balancing efficacy and tolerability is challenging in oncology, as standard dosing often prioritizes maximum tolerated doses over other patient needs. Here, the authors developed a predictive index to identify patients with increased probability of dose reduction in metastatic breast cancer and compared the real‐world effectiveness of reduced versus full starting doses. The results show that patients aged ≥65 and/or with Charlson comorbidity index ≥1 have an increased probability of dose reduction/toxicity and discontinuation. In these patients, reduced and full starting doses of palbociclib or ribociclib achieved comparable progression‐free and overall survival, while the younger, fitter patients benefit from full starting doses.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Despite the ongoing advancement of oncology drug development, the design of phase I clinical trials and dose selection remain predominantly based on the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) approach, which was historically developed for cytotoxic chemotherapy agents (CTAs). 1 In contrast to CTAs, molecularly targeted drugs, such as kinase inhibitors and antibodies, are more selective, exhibit a broader therapeutic window, and may achieve maximal modulation of tumor growth at doses lower than the MTD. 2 Consequently, the dose‐finding paradigm with its “more is better” approach may result in the recommendation of an unnecessarily high dose which has led to the initiation of several post‐marketing requirement studies for dose optimization. 2 In 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) launched the Project Optimus with the objective of reforming dose optimization in oncology drug development. 3 A guidance for industry has recently been released. 4 In routine clinical practice, physicians face the challenge of identifying the optimal treatment and appropriate (starting) dose, especially for elderly patients and those with comorbidities underrepresented in clinical trials. Minimizing therapy‐limiting toxicities is crucial to ensure that effective therapies are not discontinued prematurely, which may negatively impact patients' outcomes.

The current standard of care in the first‐line treatment of HR‐positive, HER2‐negative advanced breast cancer (ABC) is the combination of endocrine therapy (ET) with cyclin‐dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDKIs), that is, palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib. Although head‐to‐head phase III randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the three approved CDKIs are lacking, real‐world data suggest that these drugs have comparable effectiveness. 5 , 6

According to the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC), palbociclib and ribociclib were approved as recommended full starting doses (FSD) of 125 and 600 mg per day, respectively, for this indication. 7 , 8 Dose reductions generally occur due to adverse events, especially hematological or gastrointestinal toxicities. 9 Reduced starting doses (RSD) for patients at risk of toxicities may improve quality of life (QoL) 10 while maintaining efficacy, for example by decreasing treatment discontinuations due to toxicity. Although research has aimed to determine predictive factors for dose reduction in patients treated with CDKIs and ET, 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 there are currently no prospectively validated risk stratification models to identify patients who may benefit from an RSD.

Data from clinical and retrospective studies suggest that patients undergoing dose reductions of palbociclib and ribociclib may demonstrate equal or even superior efficacy compared to those without dose reductions. 11 , 12 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 However, evaluating the impact of dose reduction can be prone to immortal time bias, 26 which most studies fail to account for. Patients with a FSD who decease early in the study are less likely to receive a reduced dose, which hinders the assessment of whether efficacy truly differs between full and reduced doses. Moreover, patient and disease characteristics affecting dose reductions post‐baseline may also causally affect outcomes, thereby leading to time‐varying confounding if these variables are not adjusted for. Additionally, as previously mentioned, dose reductions are usually triggered by adverse events. Therefore, the hypothetical outcome of patients, had they maintained full dosage irrespective of these adverse events, may not be a meaningful estimate—it would be neither practical nor ethical to enforce such treatment strategy. We therefore resort to the comparison of the effects of a FSD with an RSD, where both compared treatment strategies do not preclude post‐baseline dose adjustments.

This real‐world analysis emulated a hypothetical randomized trial 27 on data from the prospective clinical cohort study OPAL, with palbociclib and ribociclib as the most frequently used CDKIs. We identified patient‐related factors significantly associated with dose reduction or toxicity discontinuation within the first 6 months of CDKI treatment and subsequently developed a predictive index. Stratified by this index, we compared progression‐free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) between patients with RSD versus FSD. We hypothesized that patients with an increased probability of dose reduction/toxicity discontinuation would have comparable OS and PFS when treated with RSD versus full dosing.

sec.title: Study design and cohort definition
sec.p: The clinical registry OPAL is an ongoing, open, prospective observational, longitudinal multicenter cohort study on patients with early and advanced (locally advanced and/or metastatic) breast cancer in Germany. Eligible patients are ≥18 years of age with documented diagnosis of early or advanced breast cancer at start of first systemic treatment. Inclusion is possible until up to 6 weeks after start of treatment. There are no restrictions on the type of systemic treatment. Sites participating in OPAL include outpatient practices and clinics as well as hospitals. Details on all (sequential) treatments, patient and tumor characteristics, biomarker testing, clinical and patient‐reported outcomes are collected. Patients are followed up until death or for a maximum of 5 years. Further details on the methodology of OPAL have been published previously. 6 , 28

In the present work, we analyzed data on all female patients with HR‐positive, HER2‐negative metastatic breast cancer (MBC) who received ET and either palbociclib or ribociclib as palliative first‐line treatment. Patients with switch of CDKI during first‐line treatment, or those who received another CDKI or chemotherapy agents in this line, were excluded from the present analysis. Switch of ET was allowed. Data base cut was on August 31, 2024.

sec.title: Derivation of a predictive index for dose reduction and toxicity discontinuation
sec.p: Dose reductions and treatment discontinuation due to toxicity in the real‐world setting indicate that the full dose may be too high for the respective patient. Reduced dose applications were defined as <125 mg for palbociclib (SmPC dose reduction levels of 100 and 75 mg) and <600 mg for ribociclib (SmPC dose reduction levels of 400 and 200 mg). As the probability of receiving a reduction depends on the treatment duration (i.e., therapies that last only a few cycles can only be reduced during the course of these few cycles, while treatments that take years can also be reduced at a later point), a comparison between patients with and without reduction may potentially reveal factors that contribute to prolonged therapies rather than those that lead to a reduction (i.e., immortal time bias). 26 This bias can be minimized by focusing solely on the early phase of treatment, such as the first 6 months, when most primary dose reductions occurred in our data. Therefore, the objective of this analysis was to compare patients who (1) started at RSD or (2) discontinued treatment due to toxicity and/or underwent an on‐treatment dose reduction within the first 6 months with patients without a dose reduction to identify predictive factors for dose reduction and toxicity discontinuation. For a better readability, the term “RSD/on‐treatment dose reduction/toxicity discontinuation” is hereafter referred to as “dose reduction.”

However, patients who did not remain under observation or discontinued their treatment prior to 6 months (e.g., due to progression or death) without an (observed) prior dose reduction cannot be unambiguously assigned to one of the two groups, as they could have experienced a reduction or toxicity within the first 6 months if they had remained under observation and had not discontinued their treatment. To deal with such intercurrent events, 29 we used a “hypothetical strategy” and estimate the probability of dose reduction had patients remained on treatment for at least 6 months, in other words, had all intercurrent events been eliminated. To this end, we censored patients who experienced intercurrent events and performed our analysis on the uncensored patients, weighted according to their inverse probability of being censored (i.e., we use inverse probability of censoring weighting, IPCW). This analysis thus assigns greater weight to those unambiguously assignable patients (non‐censored patients) whose characteristics are more similar to those patients who cannot be assigned to a group (censored patients). More specifically, non‐censored patients were assigned, stabilized propensity score weights, calculated using a generalized linear model 30 , 31 containing the following baseline variables as potentially predictive of outcome: age, metastases, Charlson comorbidity index (CCI), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, disease‐free interval (DFI), prior ET, number of metastases at start of treatment, estrogen receptor expression.

Additionally, a sensitivity analysis using the “while on treatment strategy” (i.e., treating non‐assignable patients as those without dose reduction) was performed to address the intercurrent event (for more information on the rationale behind this decision and the description of the methodology, please refer to Methods section of Data S1, Supporting Information).

Following the calculation of the IPCW weights, the non‐censored patients were divided into a derivation set (comprising approximately 70% of the weights) and a validation set (comprising approximately 30% of the weights) to later validate the identified predictive factors in an independent subsample of the OPAL cohort. This splitting was stratified by “reduction/toxicity within the first 6 months” (yes/no) in order to achieve a more accurate prediction assessment in the validation set. For the sensitivity analysis, no splitting was conducted.

The predictive index for dose reduction was derived based on the derivation set using backward elimination from a weighted logistic regression model. In this model, age, weight, BSA, BMI, metastases, chronic pulmonary disease, liver disease, diabetes, CCI, and ECOG served as predictor variables (Figure S2). Variable selection was based on the Akaike information criterion. 32 All variables in the final model with confidence intervals (CI) of their reduction odds ratio (OR) that do not include the value of “one” were identified as factors for an increased probability of dose reduction and incorporated into the predictive index. For the sensitivity analysis, backward elimination logistic regression was also used, though unweighted and without data splitting (and therefore without independent sample validation).

To validate our predictive index in an independent sample, the weighted positive predictive value (i.e., the probability of being reduced if our predictive index is above a certain threshold) was calculated in both the derivation and the validation sets (see Methods section of Data S1 for details).

sec.title: Progression‐free and overall survival of patients with a full versus a reduced starting dose
sec.p: The objective of this primary analysis was to compare PFS and OS between patients with FSD and RSD according to the SmPC (i.e., <125 and <600 mg for palbociclib and ribociclib, respectively). We were particularly interested in patients with an increased probability of dose reduction, since we hypothesized that RSD would not compromise outcome in these patients.

Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) using stabilized propensity score weights was used to adjust for confounding between patients with RSD and FSD. 30 , 31 For the calculation of the weights, the same variables were considered as in the IPCW analysis (see Methods section of Data S1). SMDs greater than 0.1 were used as indicators for imbalance. 33 The sample stratified by patients' predictive index for dose reduction (i.e., index = 0 vs. index ≥1) were analyzed. The stabilized propensity score weights were calculated for each subgroup separately to allow for a better balance in covariates.

PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. 34 PFS was defined as the interval between start of first‐line treatment and date of progression or death. Patients without tumor progression or death were censored at their date of last contact. OS was defined as the interval between start of first‐line treatment and date of death from any cause. Patients without documented death were censored at their date of last contact.
The main components of the hypothetical target trial emulation (i.e., direct head‐to‐head comparison or RCT) 27 were listed and are summarized in Table S1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses and data visualization were performed using R version 4.3.2 (2023‐10‐31) “Eye Holes” (Platform: x86_64‐pc‐linux‐gnu [64‐bit]). Propensity‐score weighting was performed using the WeightIt package (0.14.2), survival analyses were performed using the survival (3.4‐0) and survminer (0.4.9) packages.

sec.title: Cohort description and patient characteristics
sec.p: At data base cut on August 31, 2024, a total of 2086 patients with advanced breast cancer had been recruited into OPAL by 189 sites all over Germany (Figure 1). Starting from 955 patients with HR‐positive, HER2‐negative metastatic breast cancer, the present analysis is based on 618 patients who received either palbociclib plus ET (n = 386, 62%) or ribociclib plus ET (n = 232, 38%) as palliative first‐line treatment. A total of 215 patients (35%) underwent a dose reduction within the first 6 months of treatment including 109 patients (51%, i.e., 18% of the total population) who received an RSD. In contrast, 403 patients (65%) received the full dose without any documented reduction (Figure 1). Of those patients with a documented dose reduction, 14 patients underwent a subsequent increase in dosage within the initial 6 months of treatment. However, all following analyses revealed similar results when patients were treated as full‐dose patients.

sec.title: Predictors for dose reduction: Predictive index
Propensity score weighting
sec.p: Of the 618 patients included, 70 were censored prior to 6 months without prior dose reduction. Consequently, IPCW was used to reduce selection bias (see section 2 and Methods section of Data S1). SMDs before and after weighting demonstrate an acceptable balance for the total population (Figure S1).

sec.title: Identified predictive factors and indexing
sec.p: In the derivation sample (n = 385), the variables ≥65 years and CCI ≥1 were associated with an increased probability of dose reduction with an OR of 1.82 [1.19, 2.79] for age ≥65 years and an OR of 2.12 [1.29, 3.49] for CCI ≥1 (Figure 2). Square brackets denote 95% CIs. See Figure S2 for the full model including all potentially predictive factors.

caption.p: Forest plot of predictive factors (derivation sample). Predictors that lead to a dose reduction within the first 6 months of treatment, calculated in the weighted derivation sample (n = 385). CCI, Charlson comorbidity index; CI, confidence interval.

sec.p: Based on the identified factors for dose reduction (age ≥65 years, CCI ≥1), a predictive index was developed (Figure 3). Patients <65 years with a CCI of 0 were assigned an index of 0 (low probability). Patients ≥65 years or with a CCI ≥1 were classified as having an index of 1 (intermediate probability), while those aged ≥65 years and with a CCI ≥1 were assigned an index of 2 (high probability). Of the 618 patients included in this analysis, 387 (63%) had an index ≥1, indicating an increased probability of dose reduction, while 231 patients (37%) had an index of 0, indicating a low probability of dose reduction. Of those patients with an index ≥1, 20% (n = 76) received an RSD, compared to 14% (n = 33) with an index = 0.

caption.p: Predictive index. Decision‐making process for determining the predictive index for dose reduction/RSD/toxicity discontinuation. CCI, Charlson comorbidity index; RSD, reduced starting dose.

sec.p: In the validation sample, the probability of experiencing a dose reduction within the first 6 months was 39.6% in the total population and 52.4% in patients with an index = 2 (Table S2A). A higher proportion of patients with dose reduction was also observed in the subgroup of patients receiving either palbociclib or ribociclib (Table S2B,C), suggesting that our index performs similarly for both drugs. The corresponding confusion matrices are provided in Table S2D–F.
The sensitivity analysis, including patients who had discontinued their treatment prior to 6 months as patients without dose reduction, also revealed the factors CCI and age (Figure S3).

sec.title: Progression‐free and overall survival according to probability of dose reduction
Propensity score weighting
sec.p: Unadjusted baseline characteristics of patients stratified by predictive index (0 or ≥1) and starting dose (RSD or FSD) are presented in Table S3. To reduce selection bias between patients with FSD compared to patients with RSD, IPTW was used (see section 2). The covariate balance of IPTW for the total population and stratified by predictive index (0 or ≥1) is shown in Figure S4A–C. The SMDs before and after propensity score weighting revealed a good balance for the subgroup with predictive index ≥1 (Figure S4B) and an acceptable balance for the subgroup with predictive index = 0 (Figure S4C).

sec.title: Progression‐free and overall survival of the weighted cohorts
sec.p: IPTW‐weighted outcome data are presented in Figures 4 and 5. Independent of patients' probability of dose reduction, median PFS was 25.1 [18.8, 30.2] months with RSD and 27.1 [24.1, 30.9] months with FSD (Figure 4A). For patients with an increased probability of dose reduction (index ≥1), median PFS was 30.1 [21.7, 54.0] months with RSD versus 29.3 [24.9, 32.0] months with FSD (Figure 4B). In contrast, patients with low probability of dose reduction (index = 0) had a median PFS of 17.6 [9.1, 29.8] months with RSD compared to 24.5 [19.8, 32.0] months with full dosing (Figure 4C). Median OS for patients independent of the predictive index for dose reduction was 40.9 [32.9, 60.3] months with RSD versus 49.1 [42.4, 53.6] months with FSD (Figure 5A). For patients with an elevated probability of dose reduction (index ≥1), median OS was 57.6 [40.0, NA] months with RSD compared to 43.1 [38.8, 50.3] months with FSD (Figure 5B). For patients at low probability (index = 0), median OS was 32.9 [23.1, 40.9] months with RSD versus 54.2 [48.8, NA] months with full dosing (Figure 5C). Square brackets denote 95% CIs.

sec.p: While the OS and PFS curves were found to be quite similar between RSD and FSD for patients at index ≥1, a difference between RSD and FSD was observed for patients with an index = 0, particularly in the OS curve.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The MTD paradigm for oncology drugs has been criticized for its “more is better” approach, which can result in recommended doses being unnecessarily high and poorly tolerated, potentially leading to treatment discontinuation and comprising patients' QoL due to side effects. In this real‐world setting of HR‐positive, HER2‐negative MBC, the development of a predictive index to identify patients at increased probability for dose reduction and toxicity discontinuation represents a significant advancement in optimizing treatment. Age ≥65 and presence of comorbidities were identified as independent predictors. For these patients, reducing the starting dose of palbociclib or ribociclib achieved comparable PFS and OS to starting therapy with a full dose and reducing it as necessary during the course of treatment.

Clinical trials indicate no significant loss of efficacy following CDKI dose reduction in ABC, with dose reduction rates and survival times largely comparable with those observed in this real‐world analysis. A pooled analysis of the PALOMA trials revealed that 36.9% of patients required a dose reduction of palbociclib, predominantly during the first 6 months of treatment. 13 Two publications concluded that dose adjustments of palbociclib in PALOMA‐2 reduced the severity of hematological adverse events while maintaining efficacy. 18 , 21 According to pooled data from the MONALEESA trials, dose reductions of ribociclib occurred in 41.8% of patients. 22 Remarkably, patients appeared to continue to benefit from treatment, with median PFS remaining similar between 24.8 and 29.6 months, depending on the extent of dose reduction. 19 , 22 By comparison, in the overall populations, median PFS and OS were 25.3 and 63.9 months for ribociclib in MONALEESA‐2 35 , 36 and 27.6 and 53.9 months for palbociclib in PALOMA‐2. 37 , 38 In this analysis, 35% of the total patient population underwent a dose reduction of palbociclib or ribociclib within the first 6 months of treatment. Notably, half of these patients initiated treatment on a reduced dose which, per protocol, does not occur in the clinical trial setting.

Compared to patients selected for clinical trials, those treated in routine practice often present with less favorable baseline characteristics, which can lead to differences in clinical outcomes between real‐world and clinical trial settings. Most retrospective analyses on patients treated in routine practice suggest equal or even superior effectiveness with any CDKI dose reduction, 11 , 12 , 20 , 39 which have been reported to range from 30% to 58% for palbociclib or ribociclib. 11 , 12 , 20 , 24 , 25 , 39 In a recent large retrospective analysis involving ~1300 patients from the US Flatiron Health Analytic Database, median real‐world PFS was maintained with any palbociclib dose modification (20.1 vs. 19.7 months), while median OS was significantly prolonged in the dose‐reduced group compared to that treated with the FSD (59.0 vs. 49.1 months), potentially due to longer treatment. 25 In the same study, 14.5% of patients initiated palbociclib at a reduced dose, a similar proportion to our findings of 18%. 25

Importantly, interpreting the efficacy results from these clinical trials and observational studies, however, is challenging because they either did not account for post‐baseline confounding or their study design induced immortal time bias.

The phase II AMALEE study compared RSD and FSD of ribociclib (400 vs. 600 mg), effectively eliminating the risk of these sources of bias. 23 Despite a lower overall response rate as the primary endpoint with the 400 mg dose, median PFS was similar (24.9 months for 400 mg vs. 25.1 months for 600 mg) and thus comparable to our findings (overall median PFS: 25.1 months for RSD vs. 27.1 months for FSD). The authors concluded that the use of dose‐reduced ribociclib is a viable option of alleviating adverse events. 23 , 40 Immortal time bias was explicitly addressed in a Danish real‐world retrospective study involving over 500 patients with HR‐positive, HER2‐negative MBC. 9 Results showed that dose reduction of a CDKI (palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib) within the first 12 weeks of treatment was associated with reduced OS (39.9 vs. 54.3 months). However, the authors only analyzed patients who were treated for more than the 12‐week landmark (81%). 9

It is also important to note that most of the aforementioned studies either did not adjust for confounders or only included them as covariates in a multivariate survival analysis. Furthermore, none of these studies examined patients at increased risk of toxicities.

Some studies aimed to identify predictive factors for dose reduction and/or progression in patients with ABC or MBC treated with CDKIs and ET. 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 Despite these efforts, routine clinical practice lacks definitive predictors and validated predictive indices that could assist in determining the optimal starting dosage for the individual patient. Based on the existing literature and medical expertise, the present analysis considered a range of baseline variables as potentially predictive of dose reduction and progression. Notably, age ≥65 years and CCI ≥1 were found to be associated with an increased probability of dose reduction. This is a crucial consideration, since these factors are often overlooked in clinical trials, which typically focus on younger, healthier populations. Our findings are consistent with a recent retrospective multicenter study on HR‐positive, HER2‐negative MBC, which demonstrated that age ≥65 years and a CCI ≥2 were associated with greater dosage reductions of either palbociclib or ribociclib. 41 In another real‐world setting, age (≥70 years) was also a significant predictor for dose reduction of palbociclib. 16 In the same study, comorbidities were not identified as predictors, but were the second most common reason (28.6%) for an initial dose reduction after older age (42.8%). 16 While age (≥60 years) was not correlated with palbociclib dose reductions in a single‐center, retrospective study, older patients with ABC were more likely to start palbociclib at lower doses, 14 which was also shown in the PALOMAGE study. 42 In another retrospective study, patients who underwent dose reduction were significantly older compared to those in the full‐dose group (73 vs. 67 years in median), 9 similar to the baseline age of our unadjusted cohorts (70 years with dose reduction vs. 66 years without).

By combining routinely available factors—age ≥65 years and CCI ≥1—our predictive index offers an easy‐to‐use tool for identifying patients not being suitable for treatment with full‐dose palbociclib or ribociclib. In addition to predicting dose reductions, a more accurate prediction of outcomes could also help to avoid unnecessary side effects in a considerable proportion of patients.

In the present analysis, most patients (63%) were classified with an index ≥1 (age ≥65 years and/or CCI ≥1), indicating an increased probability for dose reduction. However, only 20% of these patients started treatment with an RSD. This finding is of particular importance, as increased‐probability patients receiving an RSD showed similar outcomes to those treated with the full dose (median PFS and OS of 30.1 and 57.6 months vs. 29.3 and 43.1 months). Conversely, patients under 65, without comorbidities and a low probability of dose reduction (index = 0) showed inferior outcomes with RSD (median PFS and OS of 17.6 and 32.9 months vs. 24.5 and 54.2 months with FSD). These patients closely resemble the populations included in the dose‐finding RCTs and may be less susceptible to toxicity. Therefore, initiating treatment with the FSD appears to be the most appropriate choice for younger and fitter patients.

sec.title: LIMITATIONS
sec.p: Strengths of this work include its prospective and longitudinal design, as well as the underlying, large real‐world dataset. A major advantage is the combination of stratification for dose reduction probability with the emulation of a hypothetical target trial, which addresses imbalances between treatment groups and considers immortal time bias. Although the adjustment covariates included were chosen based on the existing literature as well as medical expertise and considered sufficient, there is still a risk that unadjusted sources of confounding could lead to biased estimates. Crucially, while RSD in the group of patients with predictive index ≥1 can be explained by observed patient covariates, initial dose reductions in the group of patients with index = 0 may be caused by unobserved variables, which therefore could not be adjusted for. Hence, the observed superiority of FSD in patients with index = 0 may be due to unobserved confounding. The IPCW balance in developing the predictive index was only acceptable. However, sensitivity analysis using an alternative method for patients discontinuing the study before 6 months without dose reduction or treatment cessation identified the same variables, suggesting the results were not due to poor balance. Additionally, the balance in the effectiveness analysis was suboptimal for the subgroup with an index = 0, but the imbalanced variables mainly involved categories with few patients (e.g., ECOG unknown), making it unlikely that these influenced the significant differences in survival curves. Given the observational design of OPAL, there are no specifications concerning the timing, frequency, or criteria for tumor assessment. Therefore, PFS data should be considered as the best clinical approximation and might not be identical to the PFS determined in clinical trials. Despite the large real‐world cohort analyzed and the robust statistical design, the findings of this study may not be generalizable to other patient populations and other treatments.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: To our knowledge, this is the first real‐world analysis to combine stratification for dose reduction probability with a target trial emulation in patients with HR‐positive, HER2‐negative MBC. Our findings indicate that patients aged ≥65 years and/or with comorbidities are at an increased probability of dose reduction and discontinuation due to toxicity. These patients may benefit from initial CDKI dose reduction, as their clinical outcomes were comparable to those receiving the full dose. Younger, fitter patients under 65 without comorbidities, resembling those included in RCTs, may require the full dose to avoid poorer outcomes. Thus, a more nuanced, individualized approach to dosing warrants consideration in routine clinical practice. The predictive index developed here could serve as a valuable tool to help guide dosing, not only to improve clinical outcomes, but also to enhance patients' QoL by minimizing treatment‐limiting toxicities. Future research should aim to confirm the observed effects of an initial CDKI dose reduction and establish causal inference with greater certainty through an RCT.
